newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich admits ethics violation - "I was naive".
newsitem.headline: Gingrich admits ethics violation - "I was naive".

text.p: A House Ethics panel reported Saturday that Speaker Newt Gingrich had provided it inaccurate information in violation of House rules, and Gingrich accepted responsiblity with "great sadness."

In a finding that could hurt his chances for re-election as speaker, the panel said Gingrich had failed to seek advice on whether a college course he taught complied with laws barring use of tax-exempt foundations for partisan purposes.
It also said that Gingrich should have known that information he had provided to the subcommittee was "inaccurate, incomplete and unreliable."
Because of these failures, the panel found Gingrich in violation of a rule requiring members to act in a "a manner which shall reflect creditably" on the House.
In a statement Gingrich admitted the charges "with great sadness."

"I was overconfident, and in some ways naive," he said. "With deep sadness, I agree. I did not seek legal counsel when I should have in order to ensure complete compliance with all applicable laws and that was wrong," he said.

"In my name and over my signature, inaccurate, incomplete and unreliable statements were given to the committee, but I did not intend to mislead the committee. I accept responsibility for this and I deeply regret it."

The conclusion of the ethics panel's two-year investigation came less than three weeks before Gingrich goes before the full House as a candidate to be the first Republican speaker to be re-elected in 68 years.
The findings --the result of a two-year investigation by a four-member panel of the bipartisan ethics committee -- were certain to cast a shadow over the Jan. 7 election.
The House Republican leadership team closed ranks behind Gingrich, pledging their "unequivocal support" for his re-election.
But Democratic Whip David Bonior, Gingrich's chief critic, told a news conference Gingrich should step down. "That would be the honourable thing to do, that would be the right thing to do," he said.

The speaker is customarily elected by the majority party, with the minority voting for its own leader. Republicans have only a 20-vote margin over Democrats in the House, so Gingrich cannot afford many defections by his Republican colleagues.

The full 10-member committee must decide whether to recommend to the full House any penalty for infractions of House rules. Punishments can range from a rebuke all the way up to expulsion from the House.

The charges centred on the activities of GOPAC, a political action committee formerly headed by Gingrich, his college course called "Renewing American Civilisation" and the role played by tax-exempt nonprofit foundations.
The report took no position on allegations that Gingricvh had violated federal law in using funds raised by the tax-exempt foundations for partisan political purposes.

It said an expert in the law had told the panel that Gingrich's activities had violated the foundations' tax-exempt status and were intended to benefit Gingrich, GOPAC and other Republican entities and candidates.
But it said Gingrich's tax counsel did not agree with this asessment.
However, the report said, both agreed that had they been consulted in advance, they would have advised against using the tax-exempt groups.

But it said when it asked the speaker for more information on allegations of misuse of tax-exempt organisations, Gingrich's lawyer responded with letters denying any links between GOPAC and the "Renewing American Civilisation" course.
Gingrich should have known the information provided was "inaccurate, incomplete and unreliable," the report said.

Earlier this week, Gingrich's lawyer, Jan Baran, in an apparent dispute over the information provided to investigators, said he was longer representing the speaker before the ethics committee. A Gingrich confidant, Representative John Linder, R-Georgia, said the lawyer was to blame for providing the inaccurate information.

The subcommittee took no position on whether the tax laws had been broken. But the report contained extensive details of the political nature of of Gingrich's college course and his aim to forge a Republican election victory.
